content: The 108 forms of Wu Family Tai Chi Chuan are a series of meticulously structured movements, each with a specific name and purpose. These forms are performed in a slow, deliberate manner, particularly by beginners, to enhance focus, improve physical conditioning, and familiarize practitioners with the foundational techniques of Tai Chi. The forms are also a preparatory step for more advanced martial arts training. In English, these movements are often referred to as the hand form or simply the form, while in Mandarin, they are called ch'uan (拳). The forms are designed to cultivate concentration, strengthen the body, and introduce students to a repertoire of motion techniques. Additionally, there are solo weapon forms and shorter, repetitive sequences aimed at training power generation and energy flow (ch'i kung). Wu-style Tai Chi also includes one-person drill routines for pushing hands, which serve similar functions to power generation drills. Different schools of Tai Chi may have variations in their enumeration and translation of the forms. For example, the Shanghai branch of the Wu family uses a numbering system with 89 posture names for the same long form sequence, compared to the 108 postures used by other branches. Despite these differences, the individual posture names remain largely consistent across schools. The 108 postures of the Wu Family Tai Chi Chuan are as follows: 1.
